$comment: Everyday stories, nouns Pack file (the keywords of a pack.json) and Pack (packRef, localModelRef), one part. Same style rules as stories-pilot.json. Owner reviews each part.

stories.localModelRef.$ref: A pack with two hundred concepts in one file is hard to read. A reference lets each one live in its own small file. This keyword is the relative path of the file that holds the item. It must end in .json and stay inside the pack's folder.
stories.packRef.$ref: A shop keeps the pack it is working on in a folder next to its model. This keyword is the relative path of that pack file. It is the local alternative to a remote address, and the two cannot be used together.
stories.packRef.allowSideBySide: Two libraries a shop uses each depend on a different major version of the same pack, and NPDev normally refuses that. Allow side by side tolerates it for this direct import. It needs an alias, so the direct one stays distinguishable from the other.
stories.packRef.as: Two packs from different authors might share a name, or a name might be too long to write in every reference. As gives the pack a short name of your own, used as its prefix in this model.
stories.packRef.from: A pack lives in a registry or in a git repository, and the model has to say where to fetch it. From is that remote address, with its version tag. It cannot be combined with a local file reference.
stories.pack:$schema: A person writing a pack by hand loves it when the editor suggests the right keywords. This is the address of the JSON schema the editor reads for that help. It changes nothing in the pack itself.
stories.pack:augments: A shop needs one more box on the customer concept of a CRM pack, and a new kind of thing would be too much. Augments says this pack adds to a concept owned by another pack. The additions are additive only, and NPDev refuses collisions and sealed concepts.
stories.pack:author: People trust a pack more when they know who made it. Author is a free-text line saying who published the pack.
stories.pack:capabilities: A pack for payments brings the abilities to charge and refund. Capabilities are the outside abilities the pack contributes, written inline or kept in files of their own.
stories.pack:category: The pack store groups packs the way a supermarket groups shelves. Category is the shelf this pack goes on: security, web UI, crypto, bots, AI tools, finance, math or other.
stories.pack:concepts: A pack for a clinic brings 'Patient' and 'Appointment'. Concepts are the kinds of record the pack contributes, and the apps that use it refer to them with the pack's name in front.
stories.pack:conversions: When a pack's concept changes shape, say one 'name' box becomes 'first name' and 'last name', the rows already stored must be carried over. Conversions are those data-migration steps the pack contributes.
stories.pack:deprecated: A pack version has a flaw, and its author wants to say 'do not use this, use the next one'. Deprecated records since when, why and what replaces it. It is written into the pack before that version is published, never added afterwards, and the pack command that deprecates writes it.
stories.pack:description: In a catalogue of hundreds of packs, people want to know in one line what each one gives. Description is that sentence.
stories.pack:domainTypes: A pack for Brazil brings the types 'CPF' and 'CNPJ', each with its own checks. Domain types are the ready-made kinds of value the pack contributes.
stories.pack:dslVersion: The rules of the language change over time. DSL version says which version of it this pack was written in. It is required, and today it is 3.0.0.
stories.pack:events: A pack for orders announces 'order shipped' so other parts can react. Events are the events the pack contributes.
stories.pack:experiences: A pack can also bring complete ways of using it for each kind of person. Experiences are those experiences, and their names are never prefixed with the pack's name. The roles, concepts, queries and flows they refer to are.
stories.pack:extensionPoints: A pack keeps some parts private, but the author knows others may want to build on a few of them. Extension points are those names. An app may specialize them even though they are private, but may not use them directly.
stories.pack:fieldConventions: A pack could say that any box ending in 'Email' is an e-mail address, so nobody has to repeat it. Field conventions are those naming rules: a match and what it implies for a box that declares no type. They rank below the app's own rules.
stories.pack:firstPublishedVersion: People upgrading a pack need to know where its history begins. First published version is the pack's true first release, written once by the publish command, so the chain of migrations has a starting point.
stories.pack:flows: A pack for orders brings the recipe 'Approve order'. Flows are the flows the pack contributes.
stories.pack:forkedFrom: A shop copies a published pack and changes it. Forked from says which pack, which version and which original author it came from, so credit is given where it is due.
stories.pack:fragments: A big pack can be split into several files. Fragments lists local files whose members are merged into the pack, so the pack reads as one.
stories.pack:functions: A pack for finance brings a small calculation, such as a late-payment fine. Functions are named pure functions the pack provides, the second step of the ladder for rare needs. Others call them with the pack's name in front, and inside the pack the bare name works.
stories.pack:imports: A large company splits its system into separate areas, and one area may look at another only if it says so. Imports lists the areas this fragment may refer to. Naming one that is not listed is an error, and a cycle among the areas is an error too.
stories.pack:metadata: Whoever published the pack wants to leave a note, such as 'tested with version 4 of the app'. Metadata is a free notebook on the pack. NPDev carries it along and does nothing with it.
stories.pack:migrations: When a pack grows from 1.0.0 to 1.1.0, the apps already using it must be carried along safely. Migrations is the chain of steps for each version change. The publish command fills it in by itself when the change is harmless, and a breaking change needs real steps.
stories.pack:namespace: The code generated for a pack needs a home, and some authors care what it is called. Namespace is that optional name for the generated code.
stories.pack:pack: Every pack needs a name that is easy to type and cannot be confused, such as 'payments'. Pack is that identifier, in lower case with no spaces, and it prefixes everything the pack contributes.
stories.pack:packs: A pack for orders may be built on a pack for customers. Packs lists those dependencies, each with the version it needs, such as an exact one or 'this major version or a later minor', and optionally where to fetch it from.
stories.pack:private: A pack has helpers that are nobody else's business. Private lists the member names kept for its own use. A reference to them from outside is refused when the app is put together.
stories.pack:properties: A pack for mail brings settings such as the sender address. Properties are the settings the pack contributes.
stories.pack:propertyScopes: Some of those settings can differ by company or by branch. Property scopes are the levels the pack contributes for that.
stories.pack:queries: A pack for orders brings the question 'which orders are late'. Queries are the queries the pack contributes.
stories.pack:requires: A pack for payments needs a role that can issue refunds and an ability to reach the internet. Requires says what the pack expects from the app that uses it. If something is not provided, putting the app together is refused.
stories.pack:roles: A pack for a clinic brings the roles 'Doctor' and 'Receptionist'. Roles are the roles the pack contributes.
stories.pack:screens: A pack can also bring ready-made screens, such as a list of patients. Screens are the screens the pack contributes. Their names are never prefixed with the pack's name, but the roles, concepts, queries and flows they refer to are.
stories.pack:seeds: A pack for countries should arrive with the list of countries already filled in. Seeds are the rows created on the first start. Each one must belong to a concept the same pack declares, or putting the app together fails.
stories.pack:sequences: A pack for invoices brings the counter that gives each invoice its next number. Sequences are those document-numbering counters. Their names are not prefixed with the pack's name.
stories.pack:signature: Before installing a pack from a stranger, a careful company wants proof that nobody altered it. Signature is a cryptographic seal over the pack's content fingerprint, with the public key inside, so anyone can verify it without asking the author.
stories.pack:version: Apps must know which release of a pack they use. Version is the pack's own number, in the form major, minor and patch. It is required.
